newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak GDP seen well up, but deficit may hit growth.
newsitem.headline: Slovak GDP seen well up, but deficit may hit growth.

text.p: Slovakia's real gross GDP will rise by 5.3 to 6.7 percent with inflation at 5.2 to 6.1 percent in 1997, the Prognostics Institute (PU) of the Slovak Academy of Science predicted on Monday.
But the PU warned the country's general economic perfomance was burdened by factors such as a growing current account and trade and budget deficits.
"Slovakia's economic growth has been seriously weakened by its current account balance," forecaster and head of the Economic Institute Pavol Karasz told journalists.
"If the current account deficit continues like this the country's macroeconomic results could end in the risk zone."

Real GDP growth, boosted by credit-driven domestic demand, rose a real 7.0 percent year-on-year in the first three quarters of 1996, after a 7.4 percent growth in 1995. Slovakia's inflation rate remains at a region-low of 5.4 percent.
The institute forecast a current account deficit of 48.4 billion crowns ($1.5 bln) for 1996, after a 42 billion crown ($1.4 bln) deficit for the first 11 months of the year.

"A small open economy such as the Slovak cannot support its growth dynamics without imports dynamics," PU researcher Juraj Rencko said. "But it must be adequately covered by the export ability of the economy."
Slovakia posted a foreign trade shortfall of 64.54 billion crowns for the whole of 1996, compared with a 5.69 billion crown deficit for January-December 1995.

"Economic growth in 1997 must be linked to much lower dynamics in imports against 1996," Karasz said. "Estimated GDP growth will also require reasonable coordination between the monetary programme of the central bank and the state budget."
Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik has repeatedly criticised central bank monetary policy as too restrictive, calling its latest measures inappropriate.

The country's interbank money market rates jumped to around 27 percent at the beginning of January, after the central bank moved to rein in rapid growth in money supply and cool off the consumption-led boom.

Some analysts have said Slovakia's industrial production may crash if the rates hold at their current high levels for long, preventing even bigger companies from using short-term credits to refinance their operation.

Inflationary pressures induced by the growth of money supply in 1995, had been succesfuly eliminated last year thanks to a well-coordinated NBS monetary policy and state budget discipline, Rencko said.

"But we can say that there are no more possibilities for a further rapid decrease in inflation," he said. "The inflation rate has been, and will remain, higher than the average level of developed European economies in coming years."
